'''Charles Anthony Fusina''' (born May 31, 1957) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] for seven seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[United States Football League]] (USFL) from 1979 to 1986. He played [[college football]] for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]], and was recognized as a [[unanimous All-American]] in 1978.  Fusina played for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] and the [[Green Bay Packers]] of the NFL, and the [[Philadelphia / Baltimore Stars]] of the USFL.

'''Walter Eugene''' "'''Chuck'''" '''Foreman''' (born October 26, 1950) is an American former professional [[American football|football]]  player who was a [[running back]] for the [[Minnesota Vikings]] and the [[New England Patriots]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Considered one of the best passing-catching backs in [[History of the NFL|NFL history]],<ref name="Twin">{{cite news |url=https://www.twincities.com/2015/05/22/vikings-chuck-foreman-waits-for-call-from-hall-of-fame/ |title=Chuck Foreman waits for call from hall of fame |last=Tomasson |first=Chris |date=May 22, 2015 |newspaper=[[St. Paul Pioneer Press]] |access-date=August 6, 2018}}</ref> Foreman started in three [[Super Bowl]]s with the Vikings and was the premiere back for the team for most of the 1970s. Upon entering the league in [[1973 NFL season|1973]], he was named the [[NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year]], and he was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] for the first five seasons of his career. During this time, he was also named to the first-team [[All-Pro]] and second-team All-Pro teams two times each. Nicknamed "The Spin Doctor" for his elusive running abilities, Foreman held the Vikings franchise record for [[Carry (gridiron football)|rushing]] yards from scrimmage upon his retirement. As part of the team's 50th anniversary celebration, Foreman was named as one of the [[Minnesota Vikings#50 Greatest Vikings (2010)|50 Greatest Vikings]] in 2010.  The [[Professional Football Researchers Association]] named Foreman to the PRFA Hall of Very Good Class of 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2010.htm |title=Hall of Very Good Class of 2010 |accessdate=November 23, 2016 |archive-date=October 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181017172732/http://www.profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2010.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Foreman was raised in [[Frederick, Maryland]] and was a standout athlete in football, basketball, and track at [[Frederick High School (Maryland)|Frederick High School]]. After attending the [[University of Miami]], he was drafted 12th overall in the [[1973 NFL draft]] by the Vikings. Foreman suffered a knee injury during the [[1978 NFL season|1978 season]], after which his skills declined, and he officially retired from professional football in 1980. Following his football career, Foreman was involved with numerous business ventures in the [[Twin Cities]] area. In 2000, he was arrested for his part in a [[mail fraud]] scheme, for which he was sentenced to probation. After sentencing, he began public speaking at schools and became a substitute teacher in [[Bloomington, Minnesota|Bloomington]]. In recent years, fans and former Vikings players have been trying to get Foreman elected to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]]. Chuck is currently a weekly headline contributor to the JimBob Sports Jamboree with [[Jim Rich]], Bob Sansevere and [[Mike Morris (long snapper)|Mike "The Superstar" Morris]] a Bob FM show.<ref>{{Cite web |title=JimBob Sports Jamboree |url=https://www.mybobcountry.com/jimbob-sports-jamboree/ |access-date=2025-06-02 |website=BOB Total Country |language=en-US}}</ref>

He was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] three times, and tied the then-NFL season record for rushing [[touchdown]]s in 1981. Muncie played [[college football]] for the [[California Golden Bears football|California Golden Bears]], setting numerous school records. In his [[senior (education)|senior]] year, he was the runner-up for the [[Heisman Trophy]], given annually to the most outstanding college football player. Muncie was selected by the Saints in the first round of the [[1976 NFL draft]] with the third overall pick. He became the first member of the Saints to be named to a Pro Bowl, and he was their first player to rush for 1,000 yards. He was traded to San Diego in 1980, starring in their high-scoring offense known as [[Air Coryell]] while being named to two additional Pro Bowls. Muncie was considered one of the best running backs of his era until [[cocaine]] problems forced him into retirement. His drug problems eventually landed him in prison. Afterwards, he turned his life around by helping others through mentoring programs. He founded the Chuck Muncie Youth Foundation.

'''Charles Thomas Crist''' (January 16, 1951 – October 28, 2020) was an American professional football [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]] for the [[New York Giants]], [[New Orleans Saints]], and the [[San Francisco 49ers]].  Unusually for an NFL player, Crist never played [[college football]].

A star [[quarterback]] and defensive back in [[high school football]] and a standout on the [[basketball]] court as well in [[Salamanca, New York]] (Crist ranks second overall in Salamanca High School basketball scoring with 1,004 points, behind only Jack O'Rourke),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Sam |date=January 17, 2023 |title=Brown enters elite SHS company with 1K points |url=https://www.salamancapress.com/sports/brown-enters-elite-shs-company-with-1k-points/article_a6cbf86c-9530-11ed-a38e-6fa0e4534bb8.html |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=The Salamanca Press |language=en}}</ref> Crist received an athletic scholarship to [[Pennsylvania State University|Penn State University]]. Believing himself to be capable of playing quarterback at a high level, he insisted on playing that position if he were to play football, but Penn State coach [[Joe Paterno]] insisted he play defensive back. Rebuffing Paterno's request, Crist instead used his scholarship to play [[college basketball]], where he played four years for the Nittany Lions. Crist's reputation as a defensive back was nevertheless still high enough even after not playing college football that the Giants signed him as an [[undrafted free agent]] upon graduating in 1972. This time, he agreed to play defensive back, where he spent all seven years of his professional career, never playing quarterback again.<ref name=cshof>Kindberg, Scott (2014). [http://chautauquasportshalloffame.org/chuckcrist.php Chautauqua Sports Hall of Fame profile for Chuck Crist]. Originally written for ''[[The Post-Journal]]''. Retrieved April 6, 2016.</ref>

After retiring from professional football, he served as a high school principal and elementary school principal in the Salamanca School District. Crist spent over four years on paid leave, facing undisclosed accusations, beginning November 2009; he was exonerated February 2014.[http://www.salamancapress.com/news/article_0ccfaf72-e075-11e1-9306-001a4bcf887a.html][http://wivb.com/2014/02/17/hearing-delays-cost-taxpayers-more-than-300k/] Crist announced his retirement from school administration effective January 29, 2015, citing health problems.[http://www.salamancapress.com/news/article_067d659a-8ad9-11e4-b258-4ba7b8ef61ae.html] Prior to returning to Salamanca, Crist had also dabbled in assistant coaching with [[Cattaraugus-Little Valley Central School|Cattaraugus Central School]] from 1983 to 1985, and with the [[Alfred Saxons football]] team from 1985 to 1991.<ref name=cshof/>

Crist died October 28, 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.post-journal.com/obituaries/2020/10/charles-t-chuck-crist/|title = Charles T. "Chuck" Crist}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bradfordera.com/sports/unpretentious-crist-leaves-a-lasting-legacy/article_6de0a55e-1a4c-11eb-b3b4-278ae3abb9f7.html|title = Unpretentious Crist leaves a lasting legacy}}</ref> He was one of at least 345 [[List of NFL players with chronic traumatic encephalopathy|NFL players to be diagnosed after death with chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] (CTE), which is caused by repeated hits to the head.<ref>{{cite news |title=The driving force behind Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) |website=Concussion Legacy Foundation |url=https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |access-date=July 2, 2023 |archive-date=July 2, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702123543/https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Ken Belson and Benjamin Mueller |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/20/sports/football/cte-study-concussions-brain-tackle.html |title=Collective Force of Head Hits, Not Just the Number of Them, Increases Odds of C.T.E. The largest study of chronic traumatic encephalopathy to date found that the cumulative force of head hits absorbed by players in their careers is the best predictor of future brain disease. |work= [[The New York Times]] |date=June 20, 2023 |access-date=July 2, 2023 }}</ref>

'''Charles Edward Brown''' (born March 15, 1957) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[offensive lineman]]. He played 4 games for the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) in 1979.<ref name=pfr/> He played [[college football]] for the [[University of Houston]] Cougars.<ref name=pfr>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrowCh26.htm |title=Chuck Brown Stats |publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com |access-date=March 19, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/players/chuck-brown/ |title=Chuck Brown, C |work=Nfl.com |access-date=March 19, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://thedailycougar.com/2023/09/29/swc-rewind-trips-to-lubbock-yield-tales-of-cleats-cotton/|title=SWC Rewind: Trips to Lubbock yield tales of cleats, cotton |work=The Cougar.com |access-date=April 12, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|newspaper=Houston Post|author=Collins, Ray|date=September 29, 1977|title=This time around, UH's Brown calm for Baylor game|page=1C|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-houston-post/195470356/}}</ref>

Brown played high school football at [[Dulles High School]], where he was a [[defensive lineman]].<ref name=simmons>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|newspaper=Houston Chronicle|title=Coogs' Brown faces toughie in Simmons|author=McLaughlin, Joe|date=September 28, 1978|page=Page 2, Section 3|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-houston-chronicle/195475328/}}</ref>  He was then the University of Houston Cougars' starting [[center (football)|center]] for three seasons, 1976 through 1978.<ref name=reputation>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|newspaper=Houston Chronicle|author=McLaughlin, Joe|date=August 23, 1978|title=Cougars' Brown has reputation, now it's up to him to fill the bill|page=Page 10, Section 2|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-houston-chronicle/195470870/}}</ref> At the University of Houston, Brown was named to the [[Associated Press]] All-[[Southwest Conference]] team for 1978.<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|newspaper=Kilgore News-Herald|title=UH's Davis Heads AP All-SWC Team|date=December 3, 1978|page=3A|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kilgore-news-herald/195470104/}}</ref> He was also named the Southwest Conference Lineman of the Year that season.<ref name=pact>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|newspaper=Houston Post|author=Hollis, John|title=UH's Brown to sign pact with Oilers|page=4D|date=May 9, 1979|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-houston-post/195471249/}}</ref>

Brown was not drafted out of college.<ref name=pact/> He believed that was due to his height, at just about 6 feet.<ref name=pact/> He was signed out of college by the [[Houston Oilers]] in 1979 but was cut after one preseason game.<ref name=pact/><ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|newspaper=Houston Chronicle|title=Merkins takes on more chores|author=Lundgren, Hal|date=July 14, 1979|page=Section 3, page 1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-houston-chronicle/195469702/}}</ref><ref name=red>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|newspaper=St. Louis Post-Dispatch|title=Big Red Sign Brown|date=November 18, 1979|page=2H|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch/195469105/}}</ref> He was then signed by the Cardinals in November 1979 and added to their roster for a game against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref name=red/> After playing in 4 of the Cardinals last 5 games in 1979, he was cut by the team during the 1980 preseason.<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2026-04-13|title=Big Red cuts roster down to 60|newspaper=Belleville News Democrat|date=August 19, 1980|page=15|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-belleville-news-democrat/195469396/}}</ref>

Brown's father Charlie Brown also played for the University of Houston Cougars and signed a contract with the [[Oakland Raiders]].<ref name=reputation/><ref name=pact/>
